Then we add up those 1s as we go, which gives the page number, and finally we total each page.
questions.remember: Mark the breaks with 1, running total gives the session.
questions.why: LAG compares each event with the previous one for the same customer, and the CASE emits 1 at every session boundary, including the first row where LAG is NULL. A running SUM of those flags (default RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING frame) assigns a stable session number that GROUP BY can use. Adding INTERVAL '30' MINUTE to a DATE avoids floating-point issues from comparing date differences with 30/1440.
questions.tip: For sessionization I flag boundaries with LAG and turn them into group ids with a running SUM, the same trick used for gaps and islands.

questions.title: Asset class roll-rate matrix
questions.scenario: Rohit Agarwal in credit risk prepares a monthly roll-rate matrix for the risk committee, showing how loans moved between Standard, SMA-1, SMA-2 and NPA buckets. Loans closed during October have no October row and must show up as CLOSED, not vanish.
questions.schema:
CLASS_SEP(loan_id VARCHAR2(10), asset_class VARCHAR2(6), outstanding NUMBER(14,2))
-- classification as on 30-09-2026
CLASS_OCT(loan_id VARCHAR2(10), asset_class VARCHAR2(6), outstanding NUMBER(14,2))
-- classification as on 31-10-2026; asset_class STD, SMA1, SMA2 or NPA; outstanding in INR
questions.task: Build a matrix with one row per September class and one count column per October class (STD, SMA1, SMA2, NPA, CLOSED), rows ordered STD, SMA1, SMA2.
questions.hint: LEFT JOIN September to October, use NVL to label missing October rows as 'CLOSED', then PIVOT COUNT(*) on the October class.
questions.solution:
SELECT *
FROM  (SELECT s.asset_class AS sep_class,
              NVL(o.asset_class, 'CLOSED') AS oct_class
       FROM   class_sep s
       LEFT   JOIN class_oct o ON o.loan_id = s.loan_id)
PIVOT (COUNT(*) FOR oct_class IN ('STD' AS std, 'SMA1' AS sma1,
                                  'SMA2' AS sma2, 'NPA' AS npa,
                                  'CLOSED' AS closed))
ORDER BY DECODE(sep_class, 'STD', 1, 'SMA1', 2, 'SMA2', 3, 'NPA', 4);
questions.simple: Think of a class photo taken in September and again in October, where children may have changed sections. We make a table: rows are the September section, columns are the October section, and each box counts how many children moved that way. A child who left the school is put in a 'left' column instead of being forgotten. PIVOT turns the October section values into those columns.
questions.remember: Rows = where you were, columns = where you went.
questions.why: The LEFT JOIN keeps every September loan, and NVL maps the missing October side to 'CLOSED' so attrition is counted. PIVOT groups implicitly by every column of the source not mentioned in the PIVOT clause (here only sep_class) and returns 0 for COUNT where no rows exist. DECODE in ORDER BY imposes the business order of buckets instead of alphabetical order.
questions.tip: In a PIVOT I select only the columns I want as row keys in the inline view, because every other column becomes an implicit GROUP BY key.

questions.title: Migrate MF transactions, log bad rows
questions.scenario: Swati Kapoor is migrating legacy mutual fund transactions into the new RTA platform. Some legacy rows break constraints, and she wants the good rows loaded in one INSERT while every bad row is captured with its Oracle error for the business to fix.
questions.schema:
LEGACY_MF_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(10), folio_no VARCHAR2(10), scheme_code VARCHAR2(10), txn_type VARCHAR2(1), amount NUMBER(14,2))
-- staging copy of the old system, no constraints
MF_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(10) PRIMARY KEY, folio_no VARCHAR2(10) NOT NULL, scheme_code VARCHAR2(10), txn_type VARCHAR2(1) CHECK (txn_type IN ('P','R')), amount NUMBER(14,2) CHECK (amount > 0))
-- P = purchase, R = redemption, amount in INR
questions.output_note: ERR$_MF_TXN after the load. MF_TXN now holds 2 rows (M9001 and M9004). 1 = unique key (duplicate M9001), 1400 = NULL folio_no, 2290 = check constraint on amount or txn_type.
questions.task: Create an error log table for MF_TXN with DBMS_ERRLOG, load all rows from LEGACY_MF_TXN in a single INSERT that logs failing rows with the tag 'MIG_1611' instead of stopping, commit, and list the logged errors.
questions.hint: DBMS_ERRLOG.CREATE_ERROR_LOG creates ERR$_MF_TXN; add LOG ERRORS INTO err$_mf_txn ('MIG_1611') REJECT LIMIT UNLIMITED to the INSERT.
questions.simple: Think of a teacher checking homework copies one by one. Without error logging, one bad copy makes her throw away the whole pile. With LOG ERRORS she keeps the good copies and puts each bad one in a separate tray with a note saying what was wrong. Here the good fund transactions go into MF_TXN, and the bad ones go into ERR$_MF_TXN with their Oracle error number.
questions.remember: LOG ERRORS = good rows in, bad rows aside.
questions.why: DML error logging lets a single set-based INSERT, UPDATE, MERGE or DELETE skip rows that raise errors such as NOT NULL, CHECK, unique or conversion failures and record them, with ORA_ERR_NUMBER$, ORA_ERR_MESG$ and the tag, in the ERR$_ table. Without it, one bad row rolls back the whole statement, forcing slow row-by-row loops. The error table columns are VARCHAR2(4000), so even values that failed conversion can be stored, and the log rows persist even if the main transaction is rolled back.
questions.tip: For migrations I use LOG ERRORS REJECT LIMIT UNLIMITED so the load stays set-based and the business gets a clean list of rejected rows with reasons.

questions.title: Flatten broker trade confirmations
questions.scenario: Deepak Shetty in the back office of a stock broking firm receives exchange trade confirmations from an API as JSON. One order can be filled in several parts, and he needs one row per fill for the contract note, while rejected orders with no fills must still be visible.
questions.schema:
BROKER_CONFIRM(msg_id VARCHAR2(10), payload CLOB CHECK (payload IS JSON))
-- payload keys: trade_id, symbol, side (B/S), optional fills array of {qty, price}; price in INR
questions.output_note: BC3 has no fills array, but NESTED PATH behaves like an outer join, so the parent row still appears with NULL fill columns.
questions.task: Return one row per fill with msg_id, trade_id, symbol, side, fill_no (position in the array), qty, price and fill_value = qty * price, ordered by msg_id and fill_no.
questions.hint: Use JSON_TABLE with '$' for the order-level columns and NESTED PATH '$.fills[*]' with FOR ORDINALITY for the fills.
questions.solution:
SELECT b.msg_id, j.trade_id, j.symbol, j.side,
       j.fill_no, j.qty, j.price, j.qty * j.price AS fill_value
FROM   broker_confirm b,
       JSON_TABLE(b.payload, '$'
         COLUMNS (
           trade_id VARCHAR2(10) PATH '$.trade_id',
           symbol   VARCHAR2(20) PATH '$.symbol',
           side     VARCHAR2(1)  PATH '$.side',
           NESTED PATH '$.fills[*]'
             COLUMNS (
               fill_no FOR ORDINALITY,
               qty     NUMBER PATH '$.qty',
               price   NUMBER PATH '$.price'
             )
         )) j
ORDER  BY b.msg_id, j.fill_no;
questions.simple: Think of a tiffin box with an outer lid and small boxes inside. JSON_TABLE opens the lid and reads the label on top (trade, share, buy or sell). NESTED PATH then opens each small box inside, one row per small box, and FOR ORDINALITY numbers them 1, 2, 3. If a tiffin has no small boxes, we still write down its label with empty values, so nothing goes missing.
questions.remember: JSON_TABLE opens the box; NESTED PATH opens boxes inside.
questions.why: JSON_TABLE projects JSON into relational columns and is implicitly lateral, so it can reference b.payload from the same FROM clause. A NESTED PATH produces one child row per array element and is joined to its parent with outer-join semantics, so documents without the array still return one row with NULL child columns. FOR ORDINALITY gives the element's position, which is handy for ordering fills.
questions.tip: For arrays inside JSON I use NESTED PATH in JSON_TABLE rather than calling JSON_TABLE twice, because it keeps parents without children.

questions.title: Daily lowest and highest call rate
questions.scenario: Arvind Kulkarni on the treasury desk borrows and lends overnight in the call money market. Before the morning ALCO call he wants to see, for each day, the cheapest and the costliest rate at which deals were done.
questions.schema:
CALL_MONEY_DEAL(deal_id VARCHAR2(10), deal_date DATE, counterparty VARCHAR2(40), amount_cr NUMBER(10,2), rate_pct NUMBER(5,2))
-- amount_cr = deal amount in INR crore, rate_pct = annual interest rate in %
questions.task: For each deal date show the lowest and the highest rate_pct, sorted by date.
questions.hint: Group by deal_date and use MIN(rate_pct) and MAX(rate_pct) in the SELECT list.
questions.solution:
SELECT deal_date,
       MIN(rate_pct) AS min_rate,
       MAX(rate_pct) AS max_rate
FROM   call_money_deal
GROUP  BY deal_date
ORDER  BY deal_date;
questions.simple: Think of a class where every child writes their height on the board each day. MIN finds the shortest child and MAX finds the tallest child. GROUP BY deal_date makes a separate little group for each day. So for every day we get the lowest rate and the highest rate in one line.
questions.remember: MIN = smallest, MAX = biggest, GROUP BY = one row per group.
questions.why: MIN and MAX are aggregate functions, so GROUP BY deal_date collapses all deals of a day into one row and computes both in a single scan. Like other aggregates they ignore NULL values, and they also work on dates and strings. Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list must appear in GROUP BY.
questions.tip: MIN and MAX work on numbers, dates and text, and they skip NULLs just like SUM and AVG.

questions.title: Health claims still waiting for settlement
questions.scenario: Pooja Menon heads claims operations at a health insurer. IRDAI wants claims settled quickly, so every morning she needs the list of claims that have no settlement date yet.
questions.schema:
HEALTH_CLAIM(claim_id VARCHAR2(10), policy_no VARCHAR2(12), claim_amt NUMBER(12,2), intimated_on DATE, settled_on DATE)
-- claim_amt in INR, settled_on is NULL until the claim is paid
questions.task: List the claims that are not settled yet, oldest intimation first.
questions.hint: settled_on = NULL is never true; write settled_on IS NULL instead.
questions.solution:
SELECT claim_id, policy_no, claim_amt, intimated_on
FROM   health_claim
WHERE  settled_on IS NULL
ORDER  BY intimated_on;
questions.simple: Think of a school register where the 'returned book on' box is empty for some children. An empty box is not equal to anything, not even to another empty box. So asking 'is the box = empty?' never says yes. In SQL we must ask 'IS NULL', which means 'is this box empty?'. That gives us the claims with no settlement date.
questions.remember: Empty box? Ask IS NULL, never = NULL.
questions.why: NULL means unknown, so any comparison with NULL using =, <> or > evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only rows that are TRUE. That is why WHERE settled_on = NULL returns no rows without raising an error. IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are the only predicates that test for missing values directly.
questions.tip: I never write = NULL; comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN, so I use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

questions.title: Senior citizen FD rate eligibility
questions.scenario: Nikhil Bhosale runs the fixed deposit product at a private bank. Customers aged 60 or more get an extra 0.50% on FDs, and he wants each customer's exact age on 17-11-2026 so the rate is right even for someone whose birthday is that very day.
questions.schema:
FD_CUSTOMER(cust_id VARCHAR2(10), cust_name VARCHAR2(60), dob DATE)
-- dob = date of birth
questions.task: Show each customer's age in completed years on 17-11-2026 and label them 'Senior' if the age is 60 or more, else 'Regular'.
questions.hint: TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(DATE '2026-11-17', dob) / 12) gives completed years; dividing days by 365 goes wrong around birthdays.
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id, cust_name,
       TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(DATE '2026-11-17', dob) / 12) AS age,
       CASE WHEN MONTHS_BETWEEN(DATE '2026-11-17', dob) >= 720
            THEN 'Senior' ELSE 'Regular' END AS category
FROM   fd_customer
ORDER  BY cust_id;
questions.simple: Think of counting birthdays on a calendar instead of counting days. If your birthday is today, you have just finished one more year. MONTHS_BETWEEN counts how many months have passed since you were born, and dividing by 12 gives years. TRUNC cuts off the half-finished year, so 59 and a bit stays 59. Ramesh turns 60 today and is Senior, but Sunita turns 60 tomorrow and is still Regular.
questions.remember: Age = TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(today, dob) / 12).
questions.why: MONTHS_BETWEEN returns a whole number when both dates fall on the same day of the month, so a birthday on the reference date gives exactly 720 months and age 60. Calculations like (date - dob)/365 drift because of leap years and can label someone 60 a day or two early or late. TRUNC rather than ROUND is needed because age counts only completed years.
questions.tip: For age I use TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(ref_date, dob)/12) because dividing days by 365 breaks around birthdays and leap years.

questions.title: Turn branch return columns into rows
questions.scenario: Farhan Qureshi prepares the monthly branch return that feeds an RBI submission. The return table has one column per figure, but the validation tool needs one row per branch per figure, and a missing figure must still appear so the reviewer can chase the branch.
questions.schema:
BRANCH_RETURN(branch_code VARCHAR2(6), deposits_cr NUMBER(12,2), advances_cr NUMBER(12,2), npa_cr NUMBER(12,2))
-- October 2026 figures in INR crore; NULL = branch has not submitted that figure
questions.task: Return branch_code, metric ('DEPOSITS', 'ADVANCES' or 'NPA') and value_cr, one row per branch per metric, keeping rows where the value is missing. Sort by branch_code and metric.
questions.hint: UNPIVOT drops NULL values by default; add INCLUDE NULLS to keep B102's missing NPA row.
questions.solution:
SELECT branch_code, metric, value_cr
FROM   branch_return
UNPIVOT INCLUDE NULLS (
  value_cr FOR metric IN (deposits_cr AS 'DEPOSITS',
                          advances_cr AS 'ADVANCES',
                          npa_cr      AS 'NPA')
)
ORDER  BY branch_code, metric;
questions.simple: Think of a marks card where each subject is written side by side in one line. UNPIVOT rewrites it as a list, one line per subject, like 'Maths 80', 'Science 75'. Normally, if a subject has no mark, that line is quietly left out. INCLUDE NULLS keeps the empty line, so the teacher can see that a mark is missing.
questions.remember: UNPIVOT = columns to rows; INCLUDE NULLS keeps the blanks.
questions.why: UNPIVOT rotates the listed columns into two columns: one holding the value and one holding a label for the source column. By default it uses EXCLUDE NULLS, which silently removes rows whose value is NULL, so a missing regulatory figure would vanish instead of being flagged. Before UNPIVOT existed this was done with UNION ALL of one SELECT per column, which scans the table once per column.
questions.tip: UNPIVOT excludes NULLs by default, so for validation reports I add INCLUDE NULLS so missing figures stay visible.

questions.title: Flag card spends far above recent average
questions.scenario: Meera Pillai in the card fraud team wants a simple velocity rule: a swipe is suspicious if it is more than 3 times the average of that card's previous 3 swipes. The current swipe must not be part of its own average, and a card's first swipe has no history.
questions.schema:
CARD_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(10), card_no VARCHAR2(16), txn_time DATE, amount NUMBER(12,2))
-- card_no is masked, amount in INR, txn_time includes the time
questions.task: For every transaction show the average of the same card's previous 3 transactions (rounded to 2 decimals) and a flag 'Y' when amount is more than 3 times that average, else 'N'.
questions.hint: Use AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card_no ORDER BY txn_time ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) so the frame stops just before the current row.
questions.solution:
SELECT txn_id, card_no, amount,
       ROUND(prev3_avg, 2) AS prev3_avg,
       CASE WHEN amount > 3 * prev3_avg THEN 'Y' ELSE 'N' END AS suspicious
FROM  (SELECT t.*,
              AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card_no ORDER BY txn_time
                                ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS prev3_avg
       FROM   card_txn t)
ORDER  BY card_no, txn_time;
questions.simple: Think of checking your shopping bills in a passbook. For each new bill, you cover it with your hand and look only at the 3 bills just above it. You work out their average and ask, 'is this new bill more than 3 times that?'. The very first bill has nothing above it, so there is no average and it is not flagged.
questions.remember: 1 PRECEDING ends the frame just before me.
questions.why: The frame ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING excludes the current row, so a large swipe cannot dilute its own baseline. Near the start of a partition the frame holds fewer than 3 rows (T807 averages only T806) and for the first row it is empty, so AVG returns NULL and the comparison is UNKNOWN, which falls to the ELSE branch. ROWS is used rather than RANGE so the frame counts physical rows, not time distance.
questions.tip: To compare a value with its own history I end the frame at 1 PRECEDING, otherwise the current row pollutes the baseline.

questions.title: Roll balances up the GL tree
questions.scenario: Sandeep Agarwal in finance control reconciles the trial balance with the balance sheet heads. The chart of accounts is a tree, balances sit mostly on leaf GLs (and sometimes on a parent by mistake), and he needs every GL's total including all accounts below it.
questions.schema:
GL_ACCOUNT(gl_code VARCHAR2(6), gl_name VARCHAR2(40), parent_gl VARCHAR2(6))
-- parent_gl is NULL for the top account
GL_BALANCE(gl_code VARCHAR2(6), balance NUMBER(16,2))
-- closing balance in INR posted directly to that GL
questions.task: For every GL account show its total balance: its own posted balance plus the balances of all accounts below it at any depth. Sort by gl_code.
questions.hint: Run CONNECT BY without START WITH so every account becomes a root, keep CONNECT_BY_ROOT gl_code, then LEFT JOIN balances and group by the root.
questions.solution:
SELECT a.gl_code, a.gl_name,
       SUM(NVL(b.balance, 0)) AS total_balance
FROM  (SELECT CONNECT_BY_ROOT gl_code AS root_gl, gl_code
       FROM   gl_account
       CONNECT BY PRIOR gl_code = parent_gl) t
JOIN   gl_account a ON a.gl_code = t.root_gl
LEFT JOIN gl_balance b ON b.gl_code = t.gl_code
GROUP  BY a.gl_code, a.gl_name
ORDER  BY a.gl_code;
questions.simple: Think of cupboard drawers inside bigger drawers. To know how much money is in a big drawer, you add its own coins plus the coins in every small drawer inside it. The query starts a walk from every drawer, writes down where the walk started, and collects every drawer it reaches. Then it adds up the coins for each starting drawer.
questions.remember: CONNECT_BY_ROOT = remember where the walk started.
questions.why: Omitting START WITH makes every row a root, so the hierarchy is expanded once per account and each descendant row carries CONNECT_BY_ROOT, the root it was reached from. Grouping by that root sums a whole subtree, including balances posted directly on non-leaf GLs like 1200. The LEFT JOIN with NVL keeps accounts whose own row has no balance.
questions.tip: For subtree totals I use CONNECT BY without START WITH and group by CONNECT_BY_ROOT, which gives every node its full rolled-up balance in one query.

questions.title: Live client positions with a materialized view
questions.scenario: Rahul Saxena runs risk at a stock broker. The margin screen recalculates net positions from the full TRADE table every few seconds and is slowing down, so he wants a materialized view that keeps net quantity per client and stock and updates itself on every commit.
questions.schema:
TRADE(trade_id VARCHAR2(10), trade_date DATE, client_id VARCHAR2(8), symbol VARCHAR2(12), side VARCHAR2(1), qty NUMBER(10), price NUMBER(12,2))
-- side B = buy, S = sell; price in INR per share
questions.output_note: CLIENT_POSITION_MV right after it is built. CL02 HDFCBANK stays with net 0 because the group still has trades. When a new trade commits, only the changed group is updated using the MV log.
questions.task: Create a materialized view log on TRADE and a REFRESH FAST ON COMMIT materialized view CLIENT_POSITION_MV with net quantity (buys minus sells) and trade count per client and symbol, then query it.
questions.hint: For a fast-refreshable aggregate MV, SUM(expr) must be accompanied by COUNT(expr) and COUNT(*), and the log needs ROWID, SEQUENCE, the used columns and INCLUDING NEW VALUES.
questions.solution:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW LOG ON trade
  WITH ROWID, SEQUENCE (client_id, symbol, side, qty)
  INCLUDING NEW VALUES;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW client_position_mv
  BUILD IMMEDIATE
  REFRESH FAST ON COMMIT
AS
SELECT client_id, symbol,
       SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'B' THEN qty ELSE -qty END)   AS net_qty,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN side = 'B' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) AS net_qty_cnt,
       COUNT(*)                                           AS trade_cnt
FROM   trade
GROUP  BY client_id, symbol;

SELECT client_id, symbol, net_qty, trade_cnt
FROM   client_position_mv
ORDER  BY client_id, symbol;
questions.simple: Think of a piggy bank with a small notebook beside it. Instead of counting every coin again each time, you write down each coin you add or take out, and then just fix the total. The MV log is that notebook, and the materialized view is the saved total. REFRESH FAST ON COMMIT means the total is fixed the moment a trade is saved.
questions.remember: MV log notes the changes; fast refresh fixes only those.
questions.why: A materialized view stores the query result as a table, so the margin screen reads a few summary rows instead of aggregating all trades. The MV log records changed rows, and with COUNT(*) and COUNT(expr) present Oracle can apply inserts, updates and deletes incrementally, even removing a group when its count reaches zero. ON COMMIT adds a little work to each trade commit, so for very high trade volumes ON DEMAND refresh at short intervals may be chosen instead; DBMS_MVIEW.EXPLAIN_MVIEW shows whether fast refresh is possible.
questions.tip: Before promising fast refresh I check DBMS_MVIEW.EXPLAIN_MVIEW, and I always add COUNT(*) and COUNT(expr) next to SUM so Oracle can refresh incrementally.

questions.concept: SKIP LOCKED with BULK COLLECT LIMIT
questions.title: Parallel workers picking NEFT payments
questions.scenario: Ankita Deshmukh supports the outward NEFT engine, where several worker sessions pick pending payments from one table. Worker W1 has already locked N901 and N902 and not committed yet; worker W2 must take the next 3 free payments without waiting and without touching W1's rows.
questions.schema:
NEFT_OUTWARD(pay_id VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(14,2), status VARCHAR2(10), worker_id VARCHAR2(5))
-- status PENDING, SENT or FAILED; amount in INR; worker_id = session that sent it
questions.output_note: NEFT_OUTWARD after W2's block commits (W1 still holds N901 and N902). With WHERE ROWNUM <= 3 instead of LIMIT 3, W2 would get only N903, because ROWNUM would pick N901-N903 first and then skip the two locked ones.
questions.task: Write W2's PL/SQL block: lock up to 3 PENDING payments in pay_id order, skipping rows locked by other sessions, mark them SENT with worker_id 'W2', and commit.
questions.hint: Open a FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED cursor and FETCH ... BULK COLLECT LIMIT 3; do not use ROWNUM <= 3, because ROWNUM is applied before locked rows are skipped.
questions.simple: Think of children picking homework copies from a pile to check. If a friend is already holding a copy, you do not stand and wait, you just take the next free one. SKIP LOCKED does exactly that for table rows. LIMIT 3 means 'keep picking until you have 3 free copies', so W2 gets N903, N905 and N906.
questions.remember: SKIP LOCKED = take the next free one, don't wait.
questions.why: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED locks rows as they are fetched and silently passes over rows locked by other sessions, so many workers can drain one queue table without blocking each other. Because ROWNUM (or FETCH FIRST) is evaluated before the lock attempt, a ROWNUM <= 3 filter can return fewer rows than asked when some are locked, so the batch size must be controlled with BULK COLLECT LIMIT on the open cursor. The locks are held until COMMIT, so closing the cursor before the FORALL update is safe.
questions.tip: For queue tables I use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED with BULK COLLECT LIMIT, not ROWNUM, because ROWNUM is applied before locked rows are skipped.

lessons.why: LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row's value unless you widen the window, a common bug in month-end and closing-rate reports.
lessons.explain: When an analytic function has ORDER BY but no frame, Oracle uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. For SUM that gives a running total, but for LAST_VALUE it means the last row seen so far is the current row, so you get the row's own value back. To get the true last value of the partition, state ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or use FIRST_VALUE with ORDER BY ... DESC. Adding IGNORE NULLS turns it into a carry-forward tool.
lessons.example:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-02' d, 83.10 rate FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-03', 83.25 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-04', 83.18 FROM dual
)
SELECT d, rate,
       LAST_VALUE(rate) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS default_frame,
       LAST_VALUE(rate) OVER (ORDER BY d
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS closing_rate
FROM r;
-- default_frame: 83.10, 83.25, 83.18   closing_rate: 83.18, 83.18, 83.18
lessons.gotcha: LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (ORDER BY d) looks right in a quick test but just echoes x on every row.
lessons.line: For a closing value per period I use LAST_VALUE with an explicit UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame, or FIRST_VALUE ordered descending, because the default frame stops at the current row.
lessons.simple: LAST_VALUE sounds like 'give me the last one', but by default it only looks from the top down to the current row, so the last one it sees is itself. To see the real last row, tell it to look all the way to the end.
lessons.remember: Tell LAST_VALUE to look to the end: UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

lessons.why: Top-N queries written with ROWNUM in the same SELECT as ORDER BY return the wrong rows, a classic interview trap and a real reporting bug.
lessons.simple: Imagine a teacher who hands out medals to the first 2 children who walk in, and only after that lines them up by height. The medal winners were never the tallest, just the first through the door. ROWNUM is that door number: Oracle gives it out before ORDER BY sorts. So sort first in an inner query, then hand out the numbers.
lessons.remember: ROWNUM is given before sorting; sort inside, filter outside.
lessons.explain: ROWNUM is assigned to each row as it passes the WHERE clause, before ORDER BY runs, so WHERE ROWNUM <= 2 ... ORDER BY bal DESC picks any two rows and then sorts just those. The fix is to sort in an inline view and apply ROWNUM outside it, or in 12c and later use ORDER BY ... FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY (or ROW_NUMBER() OVER for top-N per group). WHERE ROWNUM > 1 never returns anything, because the first row fails, so the next row becomes ROWNUM 1 again. FETCH FIRST n ROWS WITH TIES also keeps rows tied with the last one.
lessons.gotcha: SELECT ... WHERE ROWNUM <= 5 ORDER BY amount DESC returns five random rows sorted, not the top five.
lessons.line: Because ROWNUM is assigned before ORDER BY, I either sort in an inline view and filter ROWNUM outside, or simply use FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY.

lessons.why: Picking the wrong ranking function on tied values is one of the most common interview traps in top-N and Nth-highest questions.
lessons.simple: Think of a race where two runners cross the line together. ROW_NUMBER is the strict referee who still gives them 1 and 2. RANK gives both of them 1 and the next runner 3, skipping 2. DENSE_RANK gives both of them 1 and the next runner 2, without skipping. All three just put numbers on rows in the order you ask for.
lessons.remember: ROW_NUMBER unique, RANK skips, DENSE_RANK never skips.
lessons.explain: All three are analytic functions that need OVER (ORDER BY ...) and can restart per group with PARTITION BY. ROW_NUMBER always gives 1, 2, 3 even on ties, so which tied row gets the lower number is not deterministic unless you add a tie-breaker column. RANK gives tied rows the same number and then jumps (1, 1, 3), while DENSE_RANK gives the same number and continues (1, 1, 2). Use ROW_NUMBER for de-duplication or exactly-N rows, RANK for 'positions' like a competition, and DENSE_RANK for 'Nth highest distinct value'.
lessons.example:
WITH b AS (
  SELECT 'Arun' cust, 90000 bal FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Bina', 90000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Chetan', 70000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Divya', 50000 FROM dual
)
SELECT cust, bal,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC, cust) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC)       AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC)       AS drnk
FROM   b;
-- Arun 90000 1 1 1 | Bina 90000 2 1 1 | Chetan 70000 3 3 2 | Divya 50000 4 4 3
lessons.gotcha: Using ROW_NUMBER = 1 to find 'the top customer' silently drops a customer who is tied for first place.
lessons.line: I pick ROW_NUMBER when I need exactly one row per group, RANK when ties should share a position with gaps, and DENSE_RANK for Nth-highest distinct values.

lessons.why: Interviewers often ask for a total next to each detail row, and choosing GROUP BY instead of an analytic function loses the detail rows.
lessons.simple: Think of a class photo and a class report card. GROUP BY is the report card: one line per class with the total, and the children's names disappear. OVER (PARTITION BY) is the class photo with a sticker on each child showing the class total: every child is still there. Use GROUP BY for summaries and OVER when you need the details plus the total.
lessons.remember: GROUP BY squashes rows; OVER keeps every row.
lessons.explain: GROUP BY collapses all rows with the same key into one result row, so only grouped columns and aggregates can be selected. An analytic function such as SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY branch) computes the same aggregate but returns it on every input row, without reducing the row count. Analytic functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING but before the final ORDER BY, so they cannot be used in WHERE; wrap them in an inline view to filter. You can even combine both, for example SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () to get a grand total next to grouped rows.
lessons.example:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT 'Pune' branch, 'A1' acct, 5000 amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Pune', 'A2', 3000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Nagpur', 'A3', 7000 FROM dual
)
SELECT branch, acct, amt,
       SUM(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY branch) AS branch_total,
       ROUND(100 * amt / SUM(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY branch), 1) AS pct
FROM   t
ORDER  BY branch, acct;
-- Nagpur A3 7000 7000 100 | Pune A1 5000 8000 62.5 | Pune A2 3000 8000 37.5
lessons.gotcha: Putting an analytic function in the WHERE clause raises ORA-30483; filter on it in an outer query instead.
lessons.line: I use GROUP BY when I want one row per group, and SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) when I need the group total alongside every detail row.

lessons.why: Interviewers often ask when to use EXISTS or IN, and the NOT IN version silently returns nothing when the list has a NULL.
lessons.simple: Think of a teacher asking 'is there at least one homework copy from Ravi in the pile?'. EXISTS stops looking as soon as it finds one copy, it just answers yes or no. IN first makes a list of names from the pile and checks if Ravi is on it. For finding matches both give the same answer. For 'not in the pile', a blank name on the list confuses NOT IN, but NOT EXISTS still works.
lessons.remember: EXISTS asks 'any match?'; NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe.
lessons.explain: EXISTS (correlated subquery) returns TRUE as soon as one matching row is found, and the select list inside it is ignored, so SELECT 1 is common. IN compares a value with the set returned by the subquery; for positive checks Oracle usually rewrites both into the same semi-join, so performance is often identical. The difference shows with negation: if the subquery returns any NULL, x NOT IN (...) is never TRUE and the query returns no rows, whereas NOT EXISTS is evaluated row by row and is unaffected. Oracle turns NOT EXISTS (and NOT IN on NOT NULL columns) into an anti-join.
lessons.example:
WITH acct AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A2' FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A3' FROM dual
), upi_txn AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no, 500 amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT NULL, 900 FROM dual
)
SELECT a.acct_no,
       CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM upi_txn u WHERE u.acct_no = a.acct_no)
            THEN 'Uses UPI' ELSE 'No UPI' END AS upi_status
FROM   acct a
ORDER  BY a.acct_no;
-- A1 Uses UPI | A2 No UPI | A3 No UPI
-- But WHERE acct_no NOT IN (SELECT acct_no FROM upi_txn) returns no rows because of the NULL.
lessons.gotcha: NOT IN against a subquery that can return NULL gives an empty result, so use NOT EXISTS or add WHERE col IS NOT NULL inside.
lessons.line: For positive checks IN and EXISTS usually get the same semi-join plan, but for exclusions I write NOT EXISTS because NOT IN breaks when the subquery returns a NULL.

lessons.why: Interviewers like asking the difference between NVL and COALESCE, and getting it right shows you understand NULL handling and performance.
lessons.simple: Think of a shopping bill where some prices are blank. NVL says 'if the box is empty, write this instead'. NVL2 asks 'is the box filled?' and writes one word for yes and another for no. COALESCE looks along a row of boxes and takes the first one that is filled. All three help you put something sensible where a blank would be.
lessons.remember: NVL = one backup, COALESCE = first filled box.
lessons.explain: NVL(a, b) returns b when a is NULL and always evaluates both arguments, converting b to the data type of a. NVL2(a, b, c) returns b when a is NOT NULL and c when it is NULL, which is handy for flags. COALESCE(a, b, c, ...) is ANSI standard, accepts any number of arguments, returns the first non-NULL one and stops evaluating as soon as it finds it (short-circuit). COALESCE requires all arguments to be of the same data type family, so COALESCE(number_col, 'NA') raises ORA-00932 where NVL would try an implicit conversion.
lessons.example:
WITH acct AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no, 5000 od_limit, CAST(NULL AS NUMBER) temp_limit FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A2', NULL, 20000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A3', NULL, NULL FROM dual
)
SELECT acct_no,
       NVL(od_limit, 0)                   AS od_or_zero,
       NVL2(od_limit, 'Has OD', 'No OD')  AS od_flag,
       COALESCE(temp_limit, od_limit, 0)  AS effective_limit
FROM   acct
ORDER  BY acct_no;
-- A1 5000 Has OD 5000 | A2 0 No OD 20000 | A3 0 No OD 0
lessons.gotcha: NVL always evaluates its second argument, so NVL(col, slow_function()) calls the function for every row, while COALESCE calls it only when col is NULL.
lessons.line: I prefer COALESCE because it is ANSI, takes many arguments and short-circuits, and I use NVL2 when I need a different value for filled and empty cases.
